papers.title: Music Similarity Estimation from Jukebox Embeddings
papers.label: arXiv:2611.34346v1

summary.one_liner: The paper proposes JukeSim, which estimates content-based similarity between music recordings using embeddings from the Jukebox generative music model, and reports it performs on par with a learned baseline and better than older hand-designed methods across several datasets.
summary.plain: The paper looks at how to tell whether two songs sound alike using only the audio, without relying on tags, genres, or listening history. The authors use the internal numerical representations (embeddings) of Jukebox, an existing AI model that generates music, as the basis for this comparison. They report that this approach works about as well as a recent learning-based method and better than the best older hand-designed methods on several datasets, though it needs more computing power.
summary.why: Audio similarity matters for recommending new songs that have no listening history yet, the so-called cold-start problem. The paper suggests that embeddings from generative music models are a viable tool for this task, though the text gives no details on real-world deployment or how large the gains are.
summary.background:
- Content-based similarity: judging how alike two recordings sound from the audio itself, ignoring metadata such as artist, title, or genre.
- Embedding: a list of numbers that a neural network produces to represent a piece of audio, where similar sounds should get nearby numbers.
- Jukebox: a large generative model from OpenAI that produces music audio; its internal representations are reused here for comparison rather than for generating music.
- Cold-start recommendation: recommending items when there is no usage data about them yet.
- Hand-designed approaches: similarity measures built from fixed signal-processing features rather than learned from data.
- Compute cost: the processing power and time needed; the paper notes JukeSim is more expensive than the alternatives.

papers.abstract: Content-based music similarity estimation aims to provide a measure of similarity between music audio recordings, disregarding any associated metadata. This has potential applications in e.g. cold-start music recommendation scenarios, where there is no user interaction data. In this work, we propose JukeSim, a new approach to estimating musical similarity based on embeddings created by Jukebox, a generative music model. In evaluations on multiple datasets, we find that JukeSim performs on par with an existing learning-based approach, and both outperform the best hand-designed approaches, which had never been compared to recent work before. Even though the required compute for JukeSim is higher than for other measures, we demonstrate the viability of utilizing generative embeddings for this task, encouraging further research.

papers.title: Line-Level Singer Diarization in Multi-Member Pop Songs: A Benchmark, Lead-Vocal Isolation, and Song-Level Decoding
papers.label: arXiv:2611.33247v1

summary.one_liner: The paper introduces line-level singer diarization for multi-member K-pop songs, a benchmark (ColorCoded-SD) with alignment and scoring tools, and a pipeline combining lead-vocal isolation, singing-adapted speaker embeddings, and two training-free song-level decoders that improves B-cubed F1 over the standard pipeline on two datasets.
summary.plain: Fans of pop groups often mark which member sings each lyric line, but tools built for telling apart speakers in ordinary speech fail on songs with four to eight singers. The authors built a benchmark of 43 K-pop songs with line-by-line singer labels, and a method that first isolates the lead voice, then groups lines by singer using voice fingerprints and two song-level decoding steps that need no training. The method raised the grouping score by about 0.06 on both their benchmark and a second corpus.
summary.why: Attributing sung lines to singers could help search, captioning, and fan archives of group music, and the paper's error analysis points to where the remaining difficulty lies. The text does not indicate applications beyond this setting, so the wider relevance is uncertain.
summary.background:
- Speaker diarization: automatically working out "who spoke when" and grouping segments by speaker.
- Source separation / vocal isolation: splitting a mixed recording into separate parts, such as the singing voice versus the backing music.
- Speaker embedding: a numerical "voiceprint" vector summarizing how a voice sounds, used to compare segments.
- Clustering: grouping items whose voiceprints are similar, without knowing the groups in advance.
- Viterbi decoding: a method that finds the most likely sequence of labels across ordered items; "sticky" means it favors keeping the same label between neighbors.
- B-cubed F1: a score that rates how well items are grouped together with others of the same true label, balancing precision and recall.
- Training-free: the method needs no additional model training on labeled data.

papers.abstract: Fans of multi-member pop groups annotate songs line by line with the member who sings each line, but speech diarization does not transfer to this setting: a commercial diarizer finds one or two speakers in songs by groups of four to eight. We study line-level singer diarization: given a song and its lyric-line timings, group the lines by singer with no prior knowledge of the group. We release ColorCoded-SD, a benchmark of 43 K-pop songs (1,740 lines, 3-8 singers per song) built from crowd annotations verified by independent annotators, together with alignment and scoring tools, and we derive line labels for the IdolSongsJp corpus from its per-singer solo renditions for evaluation on unseen singers. Combining lead-vocal isolation with a karaoke separator, singing-adapted speaker embeddings, and two training-free song-level decoders (a sticky Viterbi pass over line order and unsupervised linking of a group's songs) improves B-cubed F1 over the standard pipeline (vocal separation, speaker embeddings, per-song clustering) by +0.058 on ColorCoded-SD (p=0.001) and by +0.066 on IdolSongsJp (p=0.003). Isolating the lead is the largest single factor wherever the separator leaves a lead voice (+0.04 to +0.06 on the same lines), and with the singers' dry studio takes two different encoders become indistinguishable; the remaining errors concentrate on short lines that carry too little audio for a voiceprint. We also report negative results (more or cleaner training data, weight editing, a song-context model, and target-singer extraction) that bound where further gains can come from.

papers.title: Investigation of generalization to unseen audio generation models in audio--text semantic-alignment score prediction
papers.label: arXiv:2611.34626v1

summary.background:
- Text-to-audio (TTA) generation: AI models that produce sound from a text description.
- Semantic alignment: how well the content of a sound matches what the text says.
- Alignment-score prediction: a trained model that outputs a number rating this match, standing in for human judgment.
- Generalization: whether a model keeps working on data unlike its training data, here audio from new generators.
- Pretrained audio encoder: a model already trained to turn audio into numerical features, which the scoring model builds on.
- Adversarial training with a gradient reversal layer: a method that trains a model to make its internal features useless for identifying which generator made the audio.
summary.one_liner: This paper studies whether learned models that score how well generated audio matches its text prompt still work on audio from text-to-audio generators they were not trained on, and tests a gradient reversal layer (GRL) adversarial training method to reduce generator-specific bias.
summary.plain: Text-to-audio systems create sound from a written description, such as "a dog barking in the rain." This paper asks whether the automatic judges that rate how well a sound matches its description still work when the sound comes from a generator they never saw during training. The authors found that such judges get worse on audio from unseen generators, and that a training trick helps in some cases but only partly removes the generator-specific clues.
summary.why: Automatic scoring is often used to compare and improve text-to-audio systems, so a judge that only works on known generators could mislead researchers about newer models. The work is relevant to anyone building fair evaluation tools for generative audio, though the text does not show how broadly the findings hold beyond the settings tested.

papers.abstract: Text-to-audio generation (TTA) requires reliable evaluation of semantic alignment between generated audio and input text. Existing learning-based alignment-score prediction models have been evaluated only on audio generated by models included in the training data, leaving their generalization to unseen generation models unexplored. In this paper, we investigate the generalization of audio--text semantic-alignment score prediction models to unseen TTA models and introduce adversarial training using a generation-model classifier with a gradient reversal layer (GRL). Experimental results show that pretrained audio encoders capture generation-model-specific characteristics and that alignment-score prediction performance degrades on audio generated by unseen TTA models. Applying the GRL improves prediction performance in some settings, although its effectiveness in suppressing generation-model-specific information is limited.

papers.title: TigerTTS: Draft-Guided Multi-Frame Parallel Speech-Token Language Model for Fast and Robust Text-to-Speech
papers.label: arXiv:2611.34241v1

summary.background:
- Text-to-speech (TTS): software that converts text into spoken audio.
- Speech tokens: short numeric codes that represent slices of audio, which a language model can predict like words.
- Autoregressive model: generates one piece at a time, each depending on the previous ones; accurate but slow for long outputs.
- Non-autoregressive model: produces all pieces at once; faster but usually less precise.
- Real-time factor (RTF): time taken to generate audio divided by the audio's length; lower is faster, so 0.05 means about 20 times faster than real time.
- Word error rate (WER) and character error rate (CER): share of words or characters a speech recognizer gets wrong on the synthesized audio; lower is better.
- Latency to first packet: delay before the first chunk of audio can be played.
- KV-cache, CUDA Graphs, and weight absorption: engineering techniques for reducing memory use and speeding up GPU inference.
summary.one_liner: TigerTTS is a text-to-speech system that uses a small non-autoregressive model to draft speech tokens for a whole utterance, then refines them with a compact autoregressive language model that predicts several frames in parallel, with reported gains in speed and in word-level accuracy.
summary.plain: This paper describes a system that turns written text into spoken audio. The main problems it targets are speech that is slow to generate, and speech that skips or repeats words. The authors first sketch a rough version of the whole sentence in one pass, then fill in the detail step by step, and they report that this makes generation much faster while keeping errors low.
summary.why: Faster, more reliable speech generation matters for voice assistants and live applications where delay is noticeable. The reported results are the authors' own benchmark comparisons on specific datasets (SEED and LibriSpeech), so independent replication would be needed before relying on the figures.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive speech-token language models enable high-quality TTS but suffer from latency growth with sequence length, word omission or repetition without explicit alignment, and fidelity limits from discrete codebooks. We present TigerTTS, a production-grade LLM TTS system built around a lightweight non-autoregressive NAR model. With explicit alignment, the NAR model drafts tokens for the entire utterance, which are refined frame-by-frame by a compact autoregressive LLM. The draft is aligned frame-for-frame with LLM targets and injected at the input, ensuring training-inference consistency. Leveraging its accuracy, the LLM predicts 12 tokens per step across 3 frames and 4 groups, while a conditional-total-correlation bound keeps parallel prediction nearly lossless. We use a codebook-free FSQ tokenizer with four parallel groups and about 1800 bps to avoid codebook collapse. The backbone keeps positional information only in input embeddings, enabling exact MLA weight absorption and a four-fold KV-cache reduction. Decoding uses CUDA Graphs with a graph-safe multinomial sampler. A Fast mode further reduces first-packet latency: the NAR generator acts as a prefix synthesizer with RTF 0.03, producing the first 500 ms before LLM decoding. With CUDA-Graph decoding, TigerTTS reaches RTF 0.05, about 20x real-time, on one GPU. Despite using a 0.15B backbone, it outperforms standard PyTorch inference of VoxCPM2 2B by 5x and CosyVoice 2 by 16x. TigerTTS achieves the lowest CER and WER on SEED, 1.09 and 1.67, and strong WER, NMOS, and speaker similarity on LibriSpeech test-clean, 2.22, 4.36, and 0.820. Fast-mode guided semantic tokens provide a well-aligned content prior, reducing dropped words, loops, and runaway generation without sacrificing speed.

papers.title: Cif-query bridging for audio-native asr transfer to visual speech recognition
papers.label: arXiv:2611.32697v1

summary.background:
- Visual speech recognition (VSR): transcribing speech from video of lips, without audio.
- Automatic speech recognition (ASR): converting speech to text; Qwen3-ASR is a pretrained audio model with a large language-model decoder.
- Paraformer: a non-autoregressive speech recognition architecture; its CIF (continuous integrate-and-fire) predictor estimates how many text tokens each stretch of input corresponds to.
- Cross-attention: a mechanism that lets one set of vectors look up and weigh information from another set.
- Character error rate (CER): share of characters transcribed wrongly; lower is better.
- CTC: a training loss that aligns input frames to output characters without explicit alignment labels.
summary.one_liner: A lightweight cross-attention bridge, driven by adaptive queries from a continuous integrate-and-fire predictor, connects a Paraformer visual speech recognition encoder to the pretrained Qwen3-ASR language decoder, reporting 7.97% CER on CMLR versus 11.78% for native Paraformer.
summary.plain: This paper is about reading speech from lip movements (video only, no sound) by reusing a model that was built for listening to audio. The lip-reading model produces many video frames, which do not fit neatly into the compact input the audio model expects, so the authors add a small connector that condenses the video into a shorter set of query points and refines them against the full frame sequence. On the CMLR test set, the reported character error rate drops from 11.78% for the original Paraformer system to 7.97% for the combined system.
summary.why: Transferring the strong language knowledge of audio speech models to silent lip reading is a practical route to better visual speech recognition, which matters for accessibility and noisy settings. The text reports ablations on bridge depth, projector initialization, adapter size and CTC supervision, but the evidence comes from one dataset (CMLR), so how far the gain generalizes is not established here.

papers.abstract: Audio-native automatic speech recognition (ASR) models provide strong speech-language priors, but their compact acoustic interfaces are mismatched with long, frame-level visual features. We propose CIF-Query Bridge, a lightweight connection from a Paraformer visual speech recognition (VSR) encoder to Qwen3-ASR. The existing visual continuous integrate-and-fire (CIF) predictor produces an input-dependent number of token-rate queries; a two-layer cross-attention bridge refines them against the complete frame sequence, and a linear adapter feeds the pretrained ASR projector and decoder. This design preserves access to uncompressed visual context while avoiding direct autoregressive processing of hundreds of video frames. On CMLR, the complete visual-only transfer system achieves 7.97% character error rate, compared with 11.78% for native Paraformer under the same test split and scoring protocol---a 3.81-point absolute and 32.3% relative reduction. Controlled ablations characterize bridge depth, projector initialization, adapter capacity, and CTC supervision. The results show that CIF-derived adaptive queries provide a compact interface for transferring audio-native ASR capability to VSR.

papers.title: SoundWeaver: Compositional Warm-Starting for Text-to-Audio Diffusion Serving
papers.label: arXiv:2603.07865v2

summary.background:
- Diffusion models generate output by starting from random noise and removing it step by step; each step is a "neural function evaluation" (NFE), and fewer steps means faster generation.
- "Warm-starting" means beginning the process from a partly denoised state instead of pure noise, so fewer steps remain.
- Neural codecs are learned compressors that turn audio into compact numerical representations.
- A contextual bandit is an adaptive method that picks among options (here, how deep to skip) based on feedback from past choices.
- Training-free means the method works on existing pretrained models without any new training.
summary.one_liner: SoundWeaver is a training-free method that speeds up text-to-audio diffusion by warm-starting generation from a prompt-conditioned acoustic prior assembled from segments of cached audio clips, with an adaptive bandit choosing the skip depth per request.
summary.plain: Generating sound from a text description with modern diffusion models takes many slow refinement steps, which adds latency. This paper proposes reusing pieces of audio that were already generated earlier: it stitches segments from a small cache of about 1,000 clips into a starting point that matches the prompt, then begins the denoising process partway through instead of from pure static. The authors report speedups of 1.48 to 3.74 times across several backbone models, with quality said to improve.
summary.why: Cutting the number of model evaluations needed per clip matters for making generative audio practical in real-time or large-scale serving. The idea of reusing acoustic structure across requests, rather than treating each generation independently, may be of interest to people working on efficient inference and caching for generative models, though the text alone does not show how well it holds up outside the reported benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Text-to-audio (T2A) diffusion models generate high-quality audio but require tens of neural function evaluations (NFEs), resulting in substantial inference latency. Existing acceleration methods primarily optimize each generation trajectory independently, even when reusable acoustic structure exists in prior examples. We introduce SoundWeaver, the first training-free framework for compositional cross example acoustic reuse. Rather than generating from pure noise, SoundWeaver constructs a prompt-conditioned acoustic prior from segments distributed across cached audios and warm-starts diffusion from an intermediate noise level. We introduce an Acoustic Composition Graph (ACG), which uses neural codec representations and segment-level identification to identify candidate cross-cache transitions and structured path search to jointly optimize prompt relevance and acoustic continuity. We further establish a warm-start error bound showing how prior quality and diffusion SNR jointly govern the admissible skip depth, motivating an adaptive contextual-bandit Skip Gater that selects the warm-start level for each request. Across T2A diffusion backbones, SoundWeaver achieves 1.48-3.74x generation speedup with only a 1K-clip cache while improving generation quality.

papers.title: Preserving Prosody in Speaker Anonymization
papers.label: arXiv:2611.28290v1

summary.background:
- Speaker anonymization: altering recorded speech so a listener or machine cannot tell who the speaker is, while keeping the words understandable.
- Prosody: the melody, rhythm, stress and pacing of speech, which signal emotion, questions, and emphasis.
- Prosody encoder: a neural network that turns prosody into a compact numerical representation.
- Speech synthesis model: a system that generates audio from a representation such as text or features.
- Privacy-preserving encoder: one trained so the representation keeps useful prosody but drops identity-revealing information.
- Tradeoff: improving privacy often costs some naturalness or expressiveness, and the paper aims to reduce that cost.
summary.one_liner: This paper plugs a pretrained, privacy-preserving prosody encoder into a speech synthesis model so that speaker anonymization keeps intended prosody (rhythm, pitch, emphasis) while hiding the speaker's identity.
summary.plain: Voice anonymization tries to hide who is speaking by changing the voice, but the way someone's pitch and timing carry meaning is also tied to their identity, so changing the voice can also scramble that meaning. This work conditions the synthesized speech on prosody features taken from a privacy-preserving encoder, and reports that listeners more reliably perceive the intended prosodic meaning while anonymization stays competitive with earlier methods.
summary.why: Speech tools that hide identity are useful for privacy in voice assistants and recordings, and losing emotional or emphasis cues would make them less usable. The text reports only a modest, competitive comparison with prior work rather than a clear leap, so its practical impact is best judged from the full results.

papers.abstract: Effective prosody modeling is essential in natural speech generation applications, but complications arise in speaker anonymization, since speaker attributes are present in acoustic correlates of prosody. Our work aims to improve previous reported tradeoffs between effective speaker obfuscation and preservation of prosodic content. To this end, we integrate an existing pretrained privacy-preserving prosody encoder into a speech synthesis model, enabling prosody-preserving speaker anonymization. By conditioning speech generation on prosody features, we find that human subjects more reliably perceive intended prosodic meaning, while anonymization performance is competitive with previous work.

papers.title: Speech Emotion Recognition Across Languages: Prosodic Patterns and Self-Supervised Learning
papers.label: arXiv:2611.29040v1

summary.background:
- Prosody: the rhythm, pitch, loudness and timing of speech, separate from the words themselves.
- ANOVA and mixed-effects models: standard statistical tests for comparing group differences while accounting for repeated measurements from the same speakers or items.
- Self-supervised learning (SSL): AI models pretrained on large amounts of unlabeled audio, which can then be adapted to specific tasks.
- Fine-tuning: a short extra round of training on labeled data to adapt a pretrained model to a new task.
- Speech emotion recognition (SER): labeling the emotion of an utterance as a whole.
- Speech emotion diarization (SED): labeling when emotions change within a longer recording, analogous to speaker diarization ("who spoke when").
- Transfer learning: using knowledge learned in one setting (here, mostly one language) in another.
summary.one_liner: A cross-language study of prosody (pitch, intensity, timing) in emotional speech in Chinese, German and English, comparing human listeners with self-supervised speech models on emotion recognition and emotion diarization.
summary.plain: This paper asks how emotion shows up in the voice across three languages: Chinese, German and English. The authors measured features like loudness and pitch, and compared how well people and AI speech models could recognize the emotion being expressed. They report that humans did better than the AI models on cross-language tasks, but that the models improved considerably after a targeted adjustment (fine-tuning) and came close to native human listeners.
summary.why: Emotion recognition that works across languages matters for voice assistants, call-center analysis and health tools that listen to speech. The text suggests that certain features, such as intensity and pitch, may be shared across languages, but the abstract alone does not show how far these findings generalize, so this is best read as a preliminary result.

papers.abstract: This study investigates the prosodic patterns of emotional speech across Chinese (CN), German (DE), and English (EN), with a focus on acoustic characteristics. Using ANOVA and mixed-effects modeling, we reveal cross-linguistic and emotion-specific prosodic patterns. A comparative analysis of Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) performance demonstrates that humans outperform Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) models in cross-lingual tasks, while SSL models show significant improvement in cross-lingual SER through an efficient fine-tuning process, achieving performance competitive with native human speakers. The study also analyzes the performance of Speech Emotion Diarization (SED) between models and humans, highlighting the effectiveness of SSL models in transfer learning scenarios. These findings emphasize the interplay between universal prosodic features (e.g., intensity, pitch) and language-specific factors. Moreover, the SSL model's outstanding performance indicates the potential value of these acoustic features in emotion processing, implying possible advancements in cross-lingual emotion recognition through refined training techniques.

papers.title: PromptTTSD: Controllable Text to Spoken Dialogue Synthesis with Open-Ended Text Descriptions
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27601v1

summary.background:
- Text-to-speech (TTS): software that turns written text into spoken audio.
- Spoken dialogue synthesis: generating a multi-turn conversation with several voices, not just one reading.
- Zero-shot voice cloning: copying a voice from a short sample without extra training for that voice.
- Prompt-based control: steering the speaking style by giving a text description (e.g., "calm, slightly sad") instead of choosing from preset labels.
- Audiobook alignment: matching audio recordings to their text so that individual spoken lines can be cut out and labeled.
- Large language model (LLM): an AI text model used here to write style descriptions from story passages.
- Proprietary vs. open-source: the comparison models are closed commercial systems; this model's code and weights are publicly released.
summary.one_liner: PromptTTSD is an open-source model for generating multi-speaker conversational speech from dialogue scripts with open-ended natural-language style control, trained on a new dataset (PromptDialog) extracted from multi-narrator audiobooks.
summary.plain: Current systems that turn written dialogue into spoken conversation struggle to make each line sound right for its moment, such as shifting tone as a conversation changes. This paper builds a large set of conversational speech from audiobooks, with style descriptions written in ordinary language and pulled from the story text by a language model. The authors then train a model, PromptTTSD, that accepts both the script and a plain-language style description.
summary.why: The work targets a real gap: most prior datasets only label style with fixed tags, which limits how expressive the output can be. The text reports that the model keeps strong basic speech quality, competes with proprietary systems on style control, and improves how well lines fit the surrounding conversation; the evaluation details are not given in the summary, so the size of these gains is unclear.

papers.abstract: Spoken dialogue synthesis aims to generate multi-turn conversational speech from dialogue scripts while maintaining speaker consistency and contextual appropriateness. However, existing models largely lack fine-grained controllability, which is critical for capturing the dynamic, context-dependent style shifts in natural conversations. While prompt-based TTS has enabled such control for single-speaker speech, existing datasets heavily rely on predefined tags, which fundamentally limits their capacity to capture open-ended styles. To address this gap, we propose a scalable pipeline for extracting conversational speech from multi-narrator audiobooks, featuring an improved two-stage alignment algorithm to preserve dialogue continuity, paired with LLM-based extraction of style descriptions directly from narrative text. We release PromptDialog, a large-scale multi-speaker conversational speech dataset comprising 8,383 hours of Chinese speech and 120 hours of English speech, with open-ended style descriptions for 79% of utterances. We further introduce PromptTTSD, a spoken dialogue synthesis model built via a prompt-aware fine-tuning strategy that integrates style prompts into text-speech interleaved sequences. PromptTTSD is an open-source spoken dialogue synthesis model that supports both zero-shot voice cloning and natural language style control. Experiments demonstrate that PromptTTSD not only maintains strong fundamental synthesis capabilities but also achieves competitive open-ended style control compared with proprietary models, and substantially improves contextual appropriateness in multi-turn dialogues.

papers.title: Neural Defend ARCAS 290M: A Robust Foundation Model for AI-Generated Audio Detection
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27784v1

summary.background:
- Voice cloning / text-to-speech (TTS): software that generates speech in a chosen voice from text.
- Voice conversion: changing one speaker's voice to sound like another.
- Deepfake audio detection: classifiers that label a recording as real or AI-generated.
- Foundation model: a large general-purpose model trained once and reused for many tasks.
- Zero-shot / fine-tuning: testing on data the model was not specifically tuned for, versus adapting it to a benchmark.
- Equal error rate (EER): a standard score where lower means the detector confuses real and fake less often.
- Benchmarks and leaderboards (e.g., ASVspoof5, SpeechFake): shared test datasets and public rankings used to compare systems.
- Codec language model: a speech generator that works on compressed audio tokens.
- Channel effects: distortion from telephone or Bluetooth transmission that can confuse detectors.
summary.one_liner: A company report presents ARCAS 290M, a frozen foundation model for detecting AI-generated speech that is claimed to generalize across generators, channels, and languages without benchmark-specific fine-tuning, evaluated on ten public benchmarks and commercial leaderboards.
summary.plain: Cheap voice-cloning tools can now copy someone's voice from a few seconds of audio, which makes scam calls and fake recordings harder to spot. This work describes a single detector model, ARCAS 290M, built by a company called Neural Defend, that is meant to tell real speech from AI-generated speech across many kinds of fakes, phone lines, and languages. The authors report strong results on several public test sets and leaderboards, though these are self-reported claims in a summary.
summary.why: Reliable detection of synthetic voices matters for fraud prevention, platform safety, and verifying media. The text, however, is a promotional-style summary without the detailed methods, error rates, or independent verification needed to judge how strong the claims are.

papers.abstract: Voice cloning now needs only seconds of audio, and detectors tuned to one dataset often fail when the generator, channel, or language changes. We introduce ARCAS 290M, Neural Defend's foundation model for detecting AI-generated audio. A single frozen production model, with no benchmark-specific fine-tuning, generalizes across text-to-speech, voice-conversion, and codec-language-model generators, telephone and Bluetooth channels, recording conditions, and languages. We evaluate it on the complete official test sets of ten public benchmarks, scoring every recording exactly as released, and against commercial systems on independent leaderboards. ARCAS 290M ranks first among all systems on the Podonos leaderboard and has the lowest equal error rate among commercial detectors on ASVspoof5. It separates real from AI-generated speech almost perfectly on ASVspoof5, SpeechFake, and ShiftySpeech, and detects nearly all AI-generated speech in Hindi, Tamil, Bengali, and Telugu. On every benchmark with a published zero-shot comparison, including in-the-wild audio, partial fakes, and the conditions hardest for the field, it surpasses the strongest reported detector by a wide margin. These results establish ARCAS 290M as a general-purpose foundation for AI-generated audio detection in fraud prevention, platform safety, and media verification.

papers.title: A Novel Dataset and Framework for Schenkerian Optical Music Recognition
papers.label: arXiv:2611.26958v1

summary.background:
- Optical music recognition (OMR): software that reads images of sheet music and recovers the notes and symbols.
- Common Western music notation (CWMN): standard printed staff notation.
- Schenkerian analysis: a method that reduces a piece to layers of harmonic and voice-leading structure, shown as graphs with slurs and other markings.
- Ensemble model: several models combined so their outputs are merged for better results.
- Hypergraph / topological neural network: a network that links groups of symbols together rather than only pairs, so it can model how symbols belong together.
- Message passing: a process where nodes in a network exchange information with neighbors to refine their predictions.
- MuNG Studio: annotation software used to label OMR data.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes an optical music recognition framework for handwritten Schenkerian analysis graphs and common Western notation, combining a cropping-based model ensemble, a topological neural network for assembling notation, a new labeled dataset of handwritten Schenkerian analyses, and an algorithm that converts semantic graphs into typeset output.
summary.plain: Music theorists often sketch Schenkerian analysis, a way of diagramming the underlying structure of a piece, by hand, then re-enter it into music software one symbol at a time. This paper describes software that reads scanned handwritten versions of these diagrams and turns them into clean, typeset digital graphs. The authors also built a new collection of labeled handwritten analyses and a method for converting the recognized structure into a standard print format.
summary.why: Handwriting-to-digital tools for music notation are a practical aid for teaching and scholarship, and the text notes that existing systems miss large symbols like phrase slurs and Schenkerian markings. The released dataset and conversion algorithm may be useful to others working on this niche, though the text does not report how well the system performs.

papers.abstract: Music theory enables performers, composers, and listeners to engage more deeply with music. Schenkerian analysis (SchA) is a particularly illustrative and widely used approach for modeling tonal structure, organizing music into hierarchical layers of harmonic and voice-leading relationships. Despite its importance in pedagogy and scholarship, producing well-formatted Schenkerian graphs remains difficult. A typical workflow might involve writing the Schenkerian analysis on paper, and then manually, painstakingly, entering each symbol by hand into music software, exporting to vector graphics, and manually refining layouts in graphical editors. Existing optical music recognition (OMR) systems for handwritten common western music notation (CWMN) can be leveraged for their ability to recognize small-scale symbols common to those in SchA. However, CWMN OMR models generally fail to recognize large symbols such as phrase slurs, struggle with dense notation, and do not recognize Schenkerian analysis markings. Thus, these models do not extend well to digitizing SchA. This paper introduces a novel framework for optical music recognition of both CWMN and SchA. Our novel contributions include (1) an ensemble model in which each individual model follows a different image-cropping scheme for improved object detection, (2) a topological neural network architecture for notation assembly, where candidate hyperedges attend to one another and perform hierarchical message passing, (3) the first dataset of labeled handwritten SchAs, gathered with novel model integration to the OMR-annotation software, MuNG Studio, and (4) the first algorithm for converting semantic Schenkerian graphs into typeset format.

papers.title: Efficient Conversational Multi-Talker ASR with Predicted Speaker-Agnostic Activity Streams
papers.label: arXiv:2611.26796v1

summary.background:
- Automatic speech recognition (ASR): software that turns audio into text.
- Diarization: working out who spoke when in a recording.
- Speaker activity: a frame-by-frame yes/no record of whether each speaker is talking.
- Conditioning: feeding extra information (here, activity signals) into a model so it focuses on a particular target.
- Word error rate (WER): the share of words transcribed wrongly; "relative" degradation means the change compared with the original error rate.
- Permutation-invariant training: a way to train a model that outputs several labelled streams without caring about their order.
- Speedup and efficiency: here, how much faster the system runs compared with a baseline.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes merging multiple speakers' voice-activity timings into two speaker-agnostic streams, predicted directly from audio in one pass, to condition a single-speaker ASR model so that recognition cost no longer grows with the number of talkers.
summary.plain: Speech recognition systems that handle several people talking at once usually need to separate who is speaking when, then run a full recognition pass for each speaker, so the cost rises with the number of participants. This paper instead groups everyone's speaking times into just two anonymous streams, predicted directly from the audio in a single step, so the recognizer only runs twice regardless of how many people are present.
summary.why: Meetings and conversations often have many speakers, and a method whose cost stays flat as the group grows could make multi-talker transcription cheaper to run. The text reports speedups and small-to-moderate accuracy losses on two meeting corpora (AMI and ICSI), but it is a single preprint and its claims rest on those datasets.

papers.abstract: Multi-talker automatic speech recognition (ASR) can be performed by conditioning a single-speaker recognizer on frame-level speaker activity. However, this approach requires a complete diarization pass to obtain the conditioning signals and one ASR pass per speaker, making both the frontend and recognition costs dependent on the number of speakers. We reduce these costs by using Heuristic Error Assignment Training (HEAT) to merge the activities of an arbitrary number of speakers into two speaker-agnostic streams. Conditioning on these streams limits recognition to two ASR passes regardless of the number of participants. Through an analysis of the resulting encoder representations, we show that under a stream-assignment heuristic suited to conversational speech, the recognizer represents a stream target much as it does a speaker target. Because the streams do not encode persistent speaker identities, we further replace the conventional sliding-window diarization and clustering frontend with a model that predicts both activity streams directly from the audio in a single pass. A combination of arrival-order and permutation-invariant training objectives over the two-stream powerset labels prevents the predictor from collapsing to identical streams. We also investigate post-hoc speaker attribution by matching decoded utterances to speaker activities within their assigned streams. Experiments on corpora with diverse conversational dynamics demonstrate a favorable efficiency--accuracy tradeoff. On AMI and ICSI, two-stream conditioning is respectively 44\% and 87\% faster than per-speaker conditioning using the same diarization frontend, with less than 2\% relative WER degradation. Direct activity prediction increases these speedups to 79\% and 132\%, with relative WER degradations of 10\% and 21\%, respectively.

papers.title: Joint Language Modeling for In-the-Wild Speech-Scene Generation with Distinct Token Representations
papers.label: arXiv:2611.25503v1

summary.background:
- Speech-scene generation: producing a single audio clip containing intelligible speech plus ambient sounds (e.g., a street, a room).
- Neural audio codec: a model that compresses audio into a short sequence of discrete tokens and can reconstruct sound from them.
- Token stream: a sequence of these discrete codes; here, separate streams for speech and for environment.
- Large language model (LLM): a model originally built for text that is here pretrained and repurposed to predict audio tokens.
- Interleaved generation: producing the two token streams alternately within one shared sequence so each can inform the other.
- In-the-wild audio: real recordings, as opposed to clean studio sources mixed together artificially.
- Intelligibility: how easily the speech can be understood.
summary.one_liner: A large-language-model framework that generates speech and background environmental sound as two separate, time-aligned token streams, using a source-aware neural audio codec and training on in-the-wild mixed recordings rather than simulated mixtures.
summary.plain: This paper is about making computers produce a realistic sound scene in which someone is talking and the surrounding environment can be heard at the same time. The authors split the audio into two parallel streams, one for speech and one for the surroundings, and use a language model to generate both, guided by a text description of the scene and the words to be spoken. They report gains in speech clarity, fit to the scene description, and audio quality over earlier methods.
summary.why: Most earlier scene-generation work mixed separately recorded sounds together, which does not match how speech and surroundings actually co-occur in real recordings. Training on real mixed recordings may make such systems more practical for film, games, and assistive audio, though the text alone does not establish how far these gains extend beyond the reported experiments.

papers.abstract: Speech-scene generation aims to synthesize intelligible target speech together with diverse environmental sounds as a coherent acoustic scene. The task is considered challenging in two respects. Speech and environmental audio differ substantially in their semantic and acoustic characteristics, yet existing approaches typically model the complete scene using a single mixed acoustic representation. At the same time, the two sounds are closely related in real-world speech scenes, whereas conventional approaches usually rely on simulated scenes mixed from independently recorded sources. We propose a large language model (LLM)-based framework for joint modeling of distinct speech and environment token streams. A source-aware neural audio codec extracts temporally aligned speech and environment tokens from mixed audio, and a pretrained LLM generates both token streams in an interleaved fashion conditioned on the natural-language scene description and speech content. This formulation preserves source-specific representations while modeling the token streams within a shared generative context. Since both streams are extracted directly from mixed recordings, the model can also be adapted to in-the-wild speech scenes without isolated sources. Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework improves speech intelligibility, scene relevance, and audio quality over existing speech-scene generation techniques, with consistent gains from real-world adaptation. We further investigate the effects of distinct token representations and interleaved generation, and analyze whether the environmental sound remains stable while speech is active and how the two streams interact.

papers.title: Beyond Intelligibility: Fine-Grained Perceptual Assessment of Dysarthric Speech with Auditory Large Language Models
papers.label: arXiv:2611.23768v1

summary.background:
- Dysarthria: a speech disorder caused by weakness or poor coordination of the muscles used for speaking, often after neurological conditions.
- Perceptual assessment: expert listeners rating speech on traits like clarity and naturalness.
- Auditory large language model (ALLM): a large AI model that takes audio as input and responds in text, guided by written prompts.
- Speech Accessibility Project (SAP): a dataset effort collecting speech from people with speech differences.
- Two-stage training: first train on broad, related data (out-of-domain), then fine-tune on the target clinical data (in-domain).
- Multi-task transfer: whether learning one rating task helps with the others.
summary.one_liner: Benchmarks four auditory large language models (ALLMs) on five clinical perceptual dimensions of dysarthric speech from the Speech Accessibility Project, using a prompt-conditioned setup with two-stage (out-of-domain then in-domain) training.
summary.plain: This paper looks at whether AI models that can listen to audio and answer questions about it can judge the speech of people with dysarthria, a condition where muscle control makes speech hard to understand or unnaturally flat. The authors tested four such models on five things clinicians listen for, such as how natural the speech sounds, whether pitch is flat, how clear it is, whether consonants are imprecise, and whether there are inappropriate pauses. They report that the leading models pick up these fine-grained differences and that each model has different strengths across the prosody (rhythm and pitch) and articulation (sound formation) measures.
summary.why: Clinicians currently rely on slow, subjective listening, and most automated tools only score one thing or use generic quality measures, so a single model that rates several clinical traits could be useful for diagnosis and rehabilitation tracking. The text does not show clinical trials or validation against clinicians' outcomes, so its practical value is still unproven.

papers.abstract: Accurate assessment of dysarthric speech is vital for clinical diagnosis and rehabilitation, yet existing automated methods rely heavily on isolated, single-task models or generic speech quality metrics that fail to disentangle heterogeneous neuromotor deficits. This work presents the first systematic investigation into adapting auditory large language models (ALLMs) for multi-dimensional dysarthric speech assessment under a unified, prompt-conditioned framework. Four representative ALLMs are benchmarked across five clinical perceptual dimensions from the Speech Accessibility Project (SAP): naturalness, monopitch, intelligibility, imprecise consonants, and inappropriate silences. To bridge generic perceptual quality and clinical evaluation, a two-stage training paradigm is explored, leveraging out-of-domain pre-training followed by in-domain clinical adaptation. Experimental results demonstrate that leading ALLMs reliably capture fine-grained pathological variations, exhibiting distinct and complementary strengths across prosodic and articulatory attributes. These findings establish ALLMs as a scalable foundation for clinical speech evaluation and provide practical insights into model selection and multi-task transfer potential.

papers.title: Harmonic Circuit: Chord Progression Lies in a Sparse Principal Information Flow in Symbolic Music Models
papers.label: arXiv:2611.24453v1

summary.background:
- Mechanistic interpretability: reverse-engineering what the parts of a neural network compute.
- Circuit discovery: finding the subset of connections that carries out a specific behavior.
- Symbolic music: music represented as text-like tokens (notes, chords) rather than audio.
- Tonic/dominant: the home chord (I) and the chord a step away from it (V) that tends to lead back home.
- Causal intervention: altering or disabling parts of the model to test whether they really drive the behavior.
- Sparse sub-network: a small fraction of the model's components that the method selects.
summary.one_liner: The paper uses circuit discovery (extracting a sparse sub-network via the Auto-Emergence algorithm) to locate the part of two symbolic music generative models, ChatMusician and MuPT, that predicts the closing tonic in a I…V→I chord progression, and checks it with causal interventions.
summary.plain: Researchers studied two computer models that generate music written as symbols, and asked which internal parts of the model handle a basic music rule: after a chord moves from the home chord to the dominant and back, the model should land on the home chord again. They pulled out a small, sparse subset of the network that seems to carry this behavior, and reported that switching that subset off or changing it disrupts the harmonic pattern, according to the text's causal-intervention check.
summary.why: Most interpretability work on circuits has been done on language models, so applying it to music is a new direction, and the authors say it is the first systematic circuit-discovery study in music. Its wider relevance is uncertain from this text alone, since it covers two models and one chord pattern.

papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) seeks to decode neural network computations into human-understandable logic. A core methodology in MI is circuit discovery: identifying the information flow in sub-networks that drive specific model behaviors. While circuit discovery has matured within Natural Language Processing (NLP), the interpretable circuits in music models remain largely unexplored. In this work, we identify a music-functional circuit within two symbolic music generative models: ChatMusician and MuPT. The music function we consider is the prediction of the terminal tonic root in a classical harmonic progression pattern $I \ldots V \rightarrow I$. We use the Auto-Emergence algorithm to extract a principal sparse sub-network as the identified circuit. Validation via causal intervention confirms that this identified circuit is a primary driver of harmonic progression behaviors in the symbolic music models. To our knowledge, this represents the first systematic circuit-discovery study conducted within the music domain. Our demo page is available at: https://ukiyo23rui.github.io/auto-emergence-demo/.

papers.title: High-Fidelity Binarized Neural Vocoder
papers.label: arXiv:2611.22593v1

summary.background:
- Vocoder: the model that generates the audio waveform from an intermediate speech representation (such as a spectrogram).
- Full-precision network: a neural network whose weights and activations use ordinary floating-point numbers (many bits each).
- Binary neural network (BNN): a network that stores and processes values as 1 bit, greatly reducing memory and arithmetic cost, but losing information.
- Mixed-precision: keeping some parts of a network at higher precision while binarizing the rest.
- Time-frequency modeling: processing sound as a grid of frequency content over time.
- Inverse problem / range-null decomposition: a way of framing waveform reconstruction as recovering a signal from partial information, split into the parts the input determines and the parts it leaves open.
- LibriTTS: a public English speech dataset; out-of-distribution tests use data unlike the training set.
summary.one_liner: BiVoC is a binary neural network (1-bit weights and activations) time-frequency vocoder that adapts a prior full-precision framework (RNDVoC) and uses a mixed-precision design to keep quality-sensitive parts at full precision.
summary.plain: Neural vocoders are programs that turn compact speech representations into audio waveforms, but the best ones are large and costly to run. This paper tries to shrink them by storing and computing with just one bit per value, a technique called binarization, which is harder because it throws away a lot of information. The authors report that their model, BiVoC, does much better than simply binarizing existing vocoders and gets close to several standard full-precision ones at much lower theoretical computing cost.
summary.why: Making high-quality speech synthesis cheap enough for small devices is a practical goal, and the text suggests binary networks could be useful in audio generation more broadly. The text reports only objective and subjective listening results on LibriTTS and some out-of-distribution sets, and "lower cost" is a theoretical figure, not a measured speed or energy saving, so real-device benefit is not established.

papers.abstract: Neural vocoders have achieved remarkable progress in high-fidelity waveform generation in recent years, but most existing methods still rely on full-precision operators, leading to non-negligible storage and computational costs during inference. Binary neural networks (BNNs) provide an alternative direction by quantizing weights and activations to 1 bit. However, directly applying binarization to neural vocoders is rather challenging as it inherently incurs severe information loss. To this end, we propose BiVoC, a BNN-oriented time-frequency neural vocoder for high-fidelity waveform generation. Building on our previous full-precision RNDVoC framework, BiVoC adapts the inverse-problem formulation, range-null decomposition, and fineto-coarse non-uniform subband modeling to the 1-bit setting. Specifically, we develop a simple binarized convolutional unit to provide stable time-frequency feature modeling under binary representations. Furthermore, we analyze the quality-complexity sensitivity of different modules and propose a mixed-precision design to retain quality-sensitive components in full precision while binarizing computation-dominant parts. Extensive experiments are conducted on LibriTTS and multiple out-of-distribution benchmarks. Both objective and subjective results demonstrate that BiVoC substantially outperforms BNN variants obtained by directly binarizing existing vocoders, while achieving competitive performance against several mainstream full-precision vocoder baselines under much lower theoretical computational cost. These results demonstrate the promising potential of BNNs in the audio generation field. Codes and pre-trained weights are available at https://github.com/Andong-Li-speech/BiVoC.

papers.title: Beyond Mimicry: Constrained Exploration with GRPO for Joint Multi-Talker ASR and Diarization under Unknown Speaker Counts
papers.label: arXiv:2611.22627v1

summary.background:
- ASR (automatic speech recognition): software that turns speech into text.
- Diarization: working out who spoke when.
- Multi-talker / overlapping speech: several people talking at the same time.
- SpeechLLM: a large language model extended to take audio as input.
- SFT (supervised fine-tuning): training a model on example input-output pairs.
- Chain-of-thought (CoT): having the model write intermediate reasoning steps before its answer.
- GRPO (group relative policy optimization): a reinforcement-learning method that scores several sampled outputs against each other and favors the better ones.
- cpWER (concatenated minimum-permutation word error rate): a transcription error rate that allows speaker labels to be matched in any order; lower is better.
- WDER (word diarization error rate): the share of words assigned to the wrong speaker; lower is better.
- Reward: a score that tells the training process how good an output is.
summary.one_liner: A two-stage training approach for speech-language models that transcribes overlapping multi-speaker audio with speaker labels and timestamps, when the number of speakers is unknown, using chain-of-thought supervised fine-tuning followed by GRPO reinforcement learning with a constraint-aware reward.
summary.plain: The paper looks at the task of writing down what several people say at once in a recording, including who said what and when, without being told how many people are talking. The authors report that standard supervised training of a speech-language model is fragile when speech overlaps heavily, producing made-up text and broken speaker or timestamp tags. They add a step where the model first estimates the speaker count, then use a reinforcement-learning method that rewards correct output and penalizes malformed structure.
summary.why: Transcribing overlapping speakers with reliable labels is a hard problem for meeting transcription and similar tools, and the reported gains come from a specific training recipe. The text reports results on two test sets (Libri3Mix and a dynamic 2+3 speaker mix) but gives no comparison to other published systems, so how much it advances the field is unclear.

papers.abstract: Joint multi-talker ASR with speaker attribution and timestamps is particularly challenging when the speaker count is unknown and the output must follow a strict structure. We observe that Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)-only alignment of SpeechLLMs is brittle under dense overlaps, often leading to burst hallucinations and malformed speaker/timestamp tags. We propose a unified two-stage generative framework: (i) CoT-augmented SFT that infers the global speaker count before transcription, and (ii) GRPO-based constrained exploration guided by a Multi-dimensional Constraint-Aware Reward (MCAR) that directly optimizes permutation-invariant accuracy while enforcing counting, temporal, and structural constraints. On Libri3Mix and a Dynamic-Mix (2+3) set (speaker count unknown at test time), our model achieves 14.52%/9.24% cpWER and 1.95%/1.12% WDER, respectively, with GRPO yielding a 35%/54% relative cpWER reduction over SFT+CoT.

papers.title: A Speech-LLM Framework for Enrollment-Free Wake-Word-Guided Target-Speaker Recognition in Complex Noisy Scenarios for Seamless Human-Machine Interaction
papers.label: arXiv:2611.19844v1

summary.background:
- Target-speaker ASR: transcribing only one chosen person's speech when others talk too.
- Speaker enrollment: recording a sample of a person's voice in advance so a system can recognize them.
- Wake word: a trigger phrase (e.g., a device's name) that starts a voice assistant listening.
- Speech-LLM: a large language model that receives audio features and outputs text, generating words one at a time.
- Cross-attention: a mechanism that lets one stream of information (here, the wake-word text) guide how another (the audio encoder) weighs its inputs.
- Character error rate: the share of characters transcribed incorrectly; lower is better.
- Synthetic data pipeline: generating training audio by mixing and simulating speech and noise, since large labeled real datasets are costly.
summary.one_liner: An enrollment-free Speech-LLM that uses the wake-word text as a lexical cue to transcribe commands from the target speaker while rejecting non-target speakers, trained with a large synthetic noisy-speech pipeline and a four-stage curriculum.
summary.plain: Voice assistants often struggle when several people talk at once or when there is background noise, and they usually need a recorded sample of the owner's voice to know whom to listen to. This paper proposes a system that instead uses the wake word itself (such as a spoken trigger phrase) as a clue to pick out the speaker who said it, then transcribes that person's following command while ignoring others. The authors report a command character error rate of 16.15%, a rejection rate of 91.56% for non-target speakers, and a combined score of 87.70%, compared with 71.70% for the best enrollment-free baseline they tested.
summary.why: Removing the need for a voice enrollment step could make speech interfaces simpler to use in noisy homes, cars, or workplaces. The reported gains are over the authors' own baselines in the text, so how well they hold on other data or real devices is not shown here.

papers.abstract: Target-speaker automatic speech recognition (TS-ASR) is essential for reliable human-machine interaction in complex acoustic environments, where overlapping speech and background noise make it difficult to identify and recognize the intended speaker. Existing approaches typically rely on speaker enrollment or cascaded processing pipelines, limiting their flexibility in practical applications. To address these limitations, we propose an enrollment-free Speech-LLM framework that leverages wake-word text as a lexical cue to guide target-speaker recognition. Specifically, a text-cue encoder extracts lexical representations from the wake word, which are integrated into a pretrained speech encoder through cross-attention to establish an implicit association between the wake-word occurrence and the target speaker. This enables the model to selectively recognize subsequent commands from the target speaker without requiring enrollment speech or explicit wake-word boundaries. Furthermore, a large language model (LLM) unifies command transcription and non-target speaker rejection within a single autoregressive framework. To improve robustness against complex acoustic interference, we develop a large-scale speech synthesis and simulation pipeline with a progressive four-stage training strategy. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves a command character error rate of 16.15% and a non-target speaker rejection rate of 91.56%, yielding a unified score of 87.70%, compared with 71.70% for the strongest enrollment-free baseline. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of wake-word-guided speaker selection and highlight the potential of integrating target-speaker recognition and rejection within a unified Speech-LLM framework for robust human-machine interaction.

papers.title: Learning from Distribution: Rethinking One-Hot Supervision for ASR and QA in Speech Language Models
papers.label: arXiv:2611.20436v1

summary.background:
- Speech language model (SLM): a large AI model that takes audio as input and produces text, often built on a text LLM.
- ASR (automatic speech recognition): converting spoken audio into written text.
- Spoken QA: answering questions about what was said in an audio clip.
- One-hot supervision: training labels that mark a single correct answer with certainty, as opposed to a spread of acceptable answers.
- Output distribution: the probabilities a model assigns to all possible next words, not just the top choice.
- Fine-tuning: further training a pretrained model on a specific task.
- Chain-of-thought (CoT): having a model write out intermediate reasoning steps before its final answer.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes Learning from Distribution (LFD), which trains a speech language model's ASR outputs to match a pretrained text LLM's full output distribution rather than a single one-hot transcript, to reduce the spoken QA degradation caused by ASR-only training.
summary.plain: Speech language models can transcribe speech and also answer questions about it, but training them only to transcribe tends to make them worse at answering questions. The authors argue this happens because transcription has one fixed correct answer, which pushes the model toward rigid, transcript-only behavior. They propose a training method that instead nudges the model's predictions toward the spread of plausible outputs a text language model would give, and report that this improves both transcription and question answering.
summary.why: Many speech systems are tuned for one narrow task, and this work points to a training-signal issue that may affect how general-purpose voice assistants balance skills. The text gives only the abstract-level claims, so the size of the gains and how well they generalize are not clear from this summary alone.

papers.abstract: Speech language models (SLMs) exhibit strong capabilities in automatic speech recognition (ASR) and general-purpose speech understanding, yet ASR-specific training often degrades spoken question answering (QA) performance. We revisit this conflict from the perspective of task-specific input--output mappings and one-hot supervision. Our findings reveal pronounced task-asymmetric effects: ASR-only training severely limits QA capability, whereas QA-only training retains reasonable ASR performance. We hypothesize that the relatively deterministic mapping of ASR, combined with single-reference supervision, biases models toward transcription-specific behavior. Motivated by this perspective, we advocate broadening ASR learning objectives while preserving recognition accuracy. We propose Learning from Distribution (LFD), which aligns speech-conditioned predictions with the conditional output distributions of a pretrained text LLM. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LFD improves both ASR and QA performance, exhibits superior data efficiency, and remains effective under full-parameter fine-tuning. CoT-ASR further supports the broader applicability of our proposed supervision principle.
